## The question this session answers

Session 0 established that the gate is rigorous about **provenance** — which
contract, which checks, which bytes, signed by whom. It is entirely indifferent
to **adequacy**.

`dr-gate` runs whatever command sits in `checks:` and compares the exit code. If
the check is worthless, it signs a receipt for worthless work, faithfully, with
a valid signature binding the right tree and the right contract. Every refusal
from Session 0 still fires correctly.

So a receipt means exactly:

> These checks ran and produced these exit codes.

And never:

> These checks were the right checks.

Nothing in the system supports that second sentence. It has to be bought at
contract-writing time, before the run — which is why this session comes first.

## Start from a known state

```{bash}
find runs -mindepth 1 ! -name .gitkeep -delete 2>/dev/null
find control/receipts -name '*.json' -delete 2>/dev/null
cp control/checks/fixtures/solution-stub.mjs working/src/slugify.mjs
git checkout -- working/test/slugify.test.mjs done/contract.yaml 2>/dev/null
echo "reset: no runs, no receipts, candidate red, test and contract pristine"
```

---

## The compare

Two lanes, same contract, same task, same starting files. One control changes:
who is allowed to decide the run is finished.

```{bash}
bash scripts/demo-compare.sh s1 --mock --seq 2>&1 \
  | sed $'s/\033\[[0-9;]*m//g' \
  | tail -14
```

`--mock` needs no API key, and `--seq` runs the lanes in sequence rather than in
tmux panes — necessary in any non-interactive shell.

The left lane trusts the worker's claim. The right lane requires a gate-verified
receipt. That is the only difference between them.

---

## The weak contract

The course ships a deliberately weak contract to attack. It is the same slugify
task and it is **schema-complete** — every required key present. It would pass
any structural validation.

```{bash}
cat sessions/s1-define-done/fixtures/weak-contract.yaml
```

Schema-complete is not attack-proof. The six questions below are the drill.

---

## The six loophole questions

The method has two hats. As **author**, the contract must speak for itself —
no verbal commentary on the side, because a cold agent gets only the file. As
**attacker**, describe the laziest, cheapest result that makes every written
check pass. Not being difficult; being an agent.

An exploit names an exact edit, command, or omission. "It is vague" is not an
exploit.

### Q1 — Could the test already be green before the change?

Yes. Check 1 is **vacuous**: it imports the module and never calls the function.
The stub only throws when `slugify()` is invoked.

Demonstrated against the untouched broken stub:

```{bash}
cp control/checks/fixtures/solution-stub.mjs working/src/slugify.mjs

echo -n "the real test:  "
node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"

echo -n "weak check 1:   "
node -e "import('./working/src/slugify.mjs').then(() => process.exit(0))" 2>/dev/null; echo "exit=$?"

echo -n "weak check 2:   "
bash -c 'node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs || echo done anyway' > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"
```

Both of the weak contract's checks are green against code that is definitively
broken. The exploit is not "cut corners" — it is **do nothing at all** and
collect a valid signed receipt.

::: {.callout-important}
## The habit this buys

**Run every check against known-broken code and watch it go red before trusting
it green.** A check never seen failing is not a check — it is a command that
happens to exit 0, and reading it cannot tell you which. Check 1 looks perfectly
reasonable on the page and is inert.

This is why the fixture ships broken on purpose, and why `green-check.sh` spends
its first assertion confirming the stub fails.
:::

### Q2 — Could the result be produced by changing a fixture?

Yes, and it is the cheapest path of all. The weak contract's `must_not_change`
lists only `control/`, so the test file is fair game. Rather than fix `slugify`,
rewrite the assertions to expect whatever the broken code already does. The test
then passes **honestly** — nothing suppressed, nothing vacuous, objective
entirely missed.

```{bash}
cp working/test/slugify.test.mjs /tmp/slugify.test.real.mjs
cp control/checks/fixtures/solution-stub.mjs working/src/slugify.mjs

cat > working/test/slugify.test.mjs <<'EOF'
import { test } from 'node:test';
test('the code is fine, trust me', () => {});
EOF

echo -n "weakened test vs broken code:  "
node --test working/test/slugify.test.mjs > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"
```

The command passes. But this is the fixture, and the gate has something the weak
contract does not:

```{bash}
node src/loop.ts open --run-id weakened > /dev/null 2>&1
node control/dr-gate.ts check weakened 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"

# restore
cp /tmp/slugify.test.real.mjs working/test/slugify.test.mjs
find runs -mindepth 1 ! -name .gitkeep -delete 2>/dev/null
```

What refused it was **not** `must_not_change`. It was a host-owned manifest:

```{bash}
cat control/checks/manifest.json
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The trap in this question

Adding the test file to `must_not_change` would **not** have closed this. The
gate parses that key and never reads it again — `grep -c must_not_change
control/dr-gate.ts` returns `0`. The fixture is safe because of
`manifest.json`, which lives in `control/` where the worker cannot write.

On my own repository there is no manifest. `protect:` is the only equivalent,
and it is the only key with force.
:::

### Q3 — Could a required case be omitted?

> `outcome: the slugify function handles special characters correctly`

Yes. **"Special characters" names no cases, so the agent picks them.**

The shipped test covers lowercasing, `&` → `and`, and collapsing runs. So
implement exactly `&`, ship, and claim the outcome truthfully. Accented Latin
(`café`), CJK, emoji, quotes, slashes, percent-encoding — all emphatically
"special," all omitted, and no written word objects.

```{bash}
cp control/checks/fixtures/solution-correct.mjs working/src/slugify.mjs
node --input-type=module -e "
const { slugify } = await import('./working/src/slugify.mjs');
for (const s of ['Rock & Roll!', 'Café Society', '日本語のタイトル', 'C++ vs C#']) {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(s).padEnd(26), '→', JSON.stringify(slugify(s)));
}
"
```

The reference implementation passes every named check and still mangles three of
those four. Nothing is broken — the contract simply never asked.

The general form: **an unenumerated set in the outcome is a quantifier with no
domain.** "Handles special characters," "improves error handling," "covers the
edge cases" — in each, the agent chooses the membership, and it will choose the
cheapest members.

The fix is not a better adjective. It is moving the enumeration out of `outcome`
and into `checks`, as named inputs with expected outputs.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Transfer to my own contract

My `tidycba2` outcome already does this — *"proves 16 of 16 headings are covered
and every case runs"* is an enumeration with a domain, not "the important
gotchas." Q3 is closed there.

Its exposure is Q2 instead: the thing counting to 16 is a script the agent
writes.
:::

### Q4 — Could the command succeed without running the check?

Yes. Check 2 ends `|| echo done anyway`. The real test runs, genuinely fails,
and the `||` discards the exit code:

```
node --test …      → exits 1   (real failure)
||                 → sees non-zero, runs the right side
echo done anyway   → exits 0
─────────────────────────────────
compound           → exits 0
```

The failure output still prints, and the gate still writes it to
`runs/<id>/check-output.txt` — legible to any human who opens it, invisible to
every mechanism in the system. Most real verification failures have this shape:
not missing evidence, but evidence nothing is looking at.

The gate does defend against suppression, with a blocklist:

```{bash}
grep -n "^const SUPPRESS" control/dr-gate.ts
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why `grep`, not `sed -n '14p'`

This chunk originally cited the line by number. An upstream commit inserted a
line above it and the citation silently began printing the gate key instead —
still a valid chunk, still rendering, quietly wrong.

Line numbers are not stable identifiers. Cite by content.
:::

Check `|| echo done anyway` against that list. Not `|| true`. Not a trailing
`exit 0`. **It sails straight through**, and the gate would sign for it. A
blocklist stops the suppression you thought of — which is the Session 4 lesson
arriving early.

## A third outcome: `inconclusive`

Upstream added `control/check-exit.ts`, which gives every check three possible
outcomes rather than two:

```{bash}
grep -nE "CheckExitOutcome =|INCONCLUSIVE_CHECK_EXIT" control/check-exit.ts
```

Exit **2** is the conventional "the check could not reach a verdict" — the
command did not run, the interpreter died, the file was missing. That is
different from "the check ran and the answer was no."

The gate stays binary: only `satisfied` is accepted. But the refusal now says
which happened:

```
check failed:       '<cmd>' exited 1, expected 0
check inconclusive: '<cmd>' returned 2, expected exit 0
```

Worth knowing for my own card, where the honest starting state is exit **1** —
the check ran and said no. A task whose check exits 2 today is a task whose
check cannot run at all, and that is a weaker starting position: it proves the
harness is missing, not that the work is undone.

---

## Rules of revision

1. Every exploit gets a revision **in the contract file**, not a verbal promise.
   A loophole closed in conversation is still open in the run.
2. Prefer a check or a `protect` entry over more adjectives. "Correctly" has
   never stopped an agent.
3. When the attacker runs dry, **freeze**. If execution later proves the contract
   wrong, that is a new contract version, a new hash, and a new run — never an
   edit in place. The gate enforces this:
   `contract hash mismatch: contract changed after the run was opened`.
